## Probability Review {.section-slide background="#43464B"}

::: section-number
01
:::


## Probability

Probability is the likelihood that an event occurs **within a specified time period**.

::: {layout-ncol="1"}
![](images/paste-62FF1911.png){width="539"}

$\frac{\# \text{Favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total # of possible outcomes}}$
:::


## Probability can be reported in different ways

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
- **Proportion / percentage:** 0.40 or 40%
- **Frequency:** 40 per 100 (or 4 per 1,000)
- **Odds:** $P/(1-P)$ (ranges from 0 to $\infty$)

<br>

**Epidemiologic terminology:**
- **Cumulative incidence (risk):** the probability of experiencing the event by time *t*
  - Examples: “1-year risk,” “5-year cumulative incidence”
:::


## Rates {.section-slide}

::: section-number
02
:::


## Rates involve person-time

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
- **Incidence (hazard) rate:** number of events per unit of **person-time**
- Rates describe **how fast** events occur
- Rates can range from 0 to $\infinity$
:::


# What is the difference between a rate and a probability? {background="#c2f0c2"}

## Rates vs. probabilities {.section-slide}

::: section-number
03
:::

::: incremental
- **Probability (risk):** chance an individual experiences an event by a specified time  
- **Rate:** speed at which events occur per unit of person-time  
- **Key distinction:** rates use **person-time** in the denominator; probabilities do not
:::


## Rate (incidence rate)

::: incremental
- $\text{Rate} = \dfrac{\# \text{events}}{\text{total person-time}}$
- Interpreted as events per unit time at risk
- Can exceed 1
:::

![](images/paste-8191B0E3.png){.fragment}



## Probability (risk)

![](images/paste-62FF1911.png){width="539"}


## Example: same study, probability vs. rate
<br>

**Study:** 100 people followed for up to 4 years; 40 deaths.

::: incremental
- **Probability (risk) over 4 years:**  
  $40/100 = 0.40$  
  *Interpretation:* 40% died within 4 years.

<br>  
  
- **Rate (if all 100 followed for 4 years)**  
  Total person-time = $100 \times 4 = 400$ person-years; $40/400 = 0.10$ deaths per person-year  <br>
  *Interpretation:* ≈1 death per 10 years of total follow-up across the study population (aggregated person time)
:::  
  
  
## Timing & censoring 
<br>

::: incremental
- Rates change when **follow-up time differs**, even if the number of events is the same
- **Censoring or dropout** reduces person-time and can increase the estimated rate
:::
:::


## Example: events happen early vs. late
<br>

**Study:** 100 people, planned follow-up = 4 years  
**Case:** 40 deaths occur in Year 1

::: incremental
- Person-time = $(40 \times 1) + (60 \times 4) = 280$ person-years  
- **Rate:** $40/280 = 0.143$ deaths per person-year  
- **Probability (risk):** $40/100 = 0.40$
:::


## When time-at-risk is not reported[^3]

[^3]: Source: @gidwaniEstimatingTransitionProbabilities2020

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
::: incremental
- When individual follow-up time is unavailable, events are often assumed to be **evenly distributed**
- This approximates equal person-time for everyone
- If events occurred earlier, the true rate would be higher (and vice versa)
:::
:::



## Summary: Rates vs. Probabilities {.section-slide}

::: section-number
04
:::

**To sum up:**

::: incremental
- **Probability**
  - Answers: *What proportion of people experience the event by time X?*
- **Rate**
  - Answers: *How fast do events occur, per unit of time at risk?*
:::

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 0.55em; line-height: 1.2;"}
| Measure | Formula | Range | Used in |
|--------|---------|-------|---------|
| **Rate** | $\dfrac{\# \text{events}}{\text{total person-time}}$ | $0$–$\infty$ | Rate matrices |
| **Probability / risk** | $\dfrac{\# \text{events}}{\# \text{people followed}}$ | $0$–$1$ | Probability matrices |
:::

## Translating between rates and probabilities {.section-slide}

::: section-number
06
:::

## Converting rates/probabilities

::: incremental
-   **Rates** are instantaneous; they represent the speed of an event happening & because speed scales linearly with time, you can multiply or divide rates when the time period changes. <br>
-   **Probabilities** are accumulated outcomes (they are cumulative & bounded between 0-1); they do not scale linearly with time. You can't have more than 100% risk; so dividing/multiplying them does not preserve the correct relationship over time. 
:::

## Another way of saying the same thing: 

-   A rate tells us how fast an event occurs; it scales with time. 
-   A probability tells us whether an event occurs within time "t"; it is cumulative & bounded. The relationship with time is non-linear because the chance of an event slows as fewer people remain at risk (i.e., why we say it's "cumulative")


## Conversions 

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
-   A standard Markov model assumes an exponential (constant-hazard) transition process, so we can easily move between rates (instantaneous) and probabilities (over a time period). 
-   In other words, the risk per unit time doesn't change over time. If the hazard were not constant (say risk increases the longer you're sick), you would need a more complex time-dependent model.  

-   It is common to use the following formula to convert [rates to
probabilities]{style="background-color: yellow;"} under a constant (exponential) hazard. 


$$
p = 1 - e^{-rt} 
$$
*p=probability* ; *r=rate* ; *t=time* 
:::

## Conversions 
<br>

[Probability to Rate]{style="background-color: yellow;"}
<br>

$$ r = \frac{-ln(1-p)} {t} $$


## Conversions 
<br>

**Example:** Consider we have a 12-month probability of 10.8% that a child under age 6 is newly diagnosed with elevated blood lead levels. If your Markov model has a 3-month cycle length, a 3-month probability is needed. 



## Conversions {.smaller}
<br>

[STEP 1]{style="background-color: yellow;"} Convert the 12-month probability to a 12-month rate (or 12-month probability to a 3-month rate) 

::: callout-note
Cannot divide/multiply probabilities 
:::

$$ r = \frac{-ln(1-p)} {t} $$


$$ r = \frac{-ln(1-.108)} {1} = 0.1142891 $$

::: callout-note
Since the time period doesn't change, the denominator is 1
:::

::: notes
Ln = log
:::

## Conversions {.smaller}
<br>

[STEP 2]{style="background-color: yellow;"} Convert the 12-month rate to a 3-month rate

$$ \frac{0.1142891}{4} = 0.02857228 $$


## Conversions {.smaller}
<br>

[STEP 2]{style="background-color: yellow;"} Convert 3-month rate to 3-month probability

$$
p = 1 - e^{-r\Delta t} 
$$

$$
p = 1 - e^{−0.02857228∗1} = 0.028168
$$

::: notes
3/12 = 1/4

If we wanted to convert to 1M rate, we would take 1/12 

*** You take # of months / 12. So, if you want a 5-year probability, you take 60/12 = 5, so multiply by 5
:::


## Conversions {.smaller}
<br>

OR, [Step 1]{style="background-color: aquamarine;"} Convert the 12-month probability to a 3-month rate

$$ r = \frac{-ln(1-p)} {t} $$

$$ r = \frac{-ln(1-.108)} {4} = 0.02857229 $$ 


## Conversions {.smaller}
<br>

[STEP 2]{style="background-color: aquamarine;"} Convert 3-month rate to a 3-month probability

$$
p = 1 - e^{-r\Delta t} 
$$

$$
p = 1 - e^{−0.02857229∗1} = 0.028168 
$$

## Conversions 
<br> 


::: callout-note
***IF we took the probability of .108 / 4 to get the 3M probability, we would get 0.027. This is CLOSE but it could make a huge difference when modeling hundredths of thousands of individuals, for example
:::


## Alternative Rate-to-Probability Conversions {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
- With longer cycle lengths (e.g., 1 year), individuals may experience **multiple transitions within a single cycle** (e.g., healthy → sick → dead).

- The standard Markov conversion  
  $p_{HS}= 1 - e^{-r_{HS}\Delta t}$  
  converts each transition **independently**, ignoring that death competes with sickness within the same time interval.

- As a result, individuals who become sick and then die within the same cycle
  **cannot be represented as experiencing both transitions**.

- In practice, this leads to **underestimation of deaths** when cycle lengths are long.

- This problem can be mitigated by using **shorter cycle lengths** or **competing-risk rate-to-probability conversions** that properly allocate transitions within each cycle.
:::


::: {.column width="50%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-align: center
//| fig-width: 4
//| fig-cap: compound Transition Patterns Using Standard Rate to Probability Conversion Formulas
//| label: fig-comp-st
digraph G {
    layout = neato;
    Healthy [pos="0,0!" style="filled" fillcolor="#81aede"];
    Sick [pos="1,1!" style="filled" fillcolor="#81aede"]; 
    Dead [pos="1,-1!"]
    Healthy -> Healthy [color="#d9d0d0"];
    Sick -> Sick [color="#d9d0d0"];
    Healthy -> Sick [color="blue" penwidth=3 ]; 
    Sick -> Dead [color="red" style="dotted" penwidth=3];
    Healthy -> Dead [color="#d9d0d0"];
    Dead -> Dead [color="#d9d0d0"];
  }
```

:::
:::

:::


## Alternative Rate-to-Probability Conversions {.smaller}

A set of formulas often used to account for competing risks are as
follows:

$$
p_{HS}= \frac{r_{HS}}{r_{HS}+r_{HD}}\big ( 1 - e^{-(r_{HS}+r_{HD})\Delta t}\big )
$$

$$
p_{HD}= \frac{r_{HD}}{r_{HS}+r_{HD}}\big ( 1 - e^{-(r_{HS}+r_{HD})\Delta t}\big )
$$

$$
p_{HH} = e^{-(r_{HS}+r_{HD})\Delta t}
$$


## What to use {.smaller}

## What to use {.smaller}

| Equation | Use case | Advantage |
|-----------|-----------|------------|
| $p = 1 - e^{-rt}$ | When you know a **rate** but need a **probability** for a fixed cycle length | Simple closed-form conversion under a constant (exponential) hazard |
| $r = -\ln(1-p)/t$ | When you have a **probability** but need a **rate** to rescale across time intervals | Preserves the correct exponential relationship when changing cycle length |
| Competing-risk formulas $p_{HS}, p_{HD}$ | When more than one event can occur from the same state (e.g., *Healthy → Sick* and *Healthy → Dead*) | Properly accounts for competing hazards and prevents hidden within-cycle events |



## Alternative Rate-to-Probability Conversions {.smaller}
<br>

There's an even more accurate way to correct for "competing risks" & while it's beyond the scope of this introductory workshop, we will briefly review how to do this within the Markov lecture. 
:::
